parsed.explanation: The combined regime offers the traveller strong documented protections: gender identity/expression protected in the national human-rights act and criminal-code hate provisions, functional recourse (a human-rights commission with published policy and case law), identity-based prison placement, and no documented trans-specific border, screening, or facility restriction. No tier-1 or tier-2 visitor exposure appears. Offsetting this: six consecutive years of rising police-reported hate crimes, a 2022 survey showing 39% of 2SLGBTQI+ people experienced identity-based violence (90% verbal), an organised anti-trans movement, and provincial school/healthcare rollbacks — mostly resident-facing but signalling social hostility. Trans-prisoner abuse reports implicate institutions, though custody rarely touches short-stay visitors. Net: reduced risk with meaningful social-hostility tail.

entry_documents.exposure: No trans-specific border or screening practice documented; national documents offer an X marker and a 2016 self-declaration update pathway (resident-facing but a climate signal).
entry_documents.protection: No documented entry refusal, marker mismatch penalty, or secondary-screening practice aimed at trans visitors.
entry_documents.interaction: Entry encounter is undocumented; an outed visitor falls back on the national human-rights act and provincial codes.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: A 2022 report alleges a pattern of abuse and discrimination against gender-diverse prisoners, including elevated sexual-assault risk; litigation over placement and gender-affirming care is recorded without outcome.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: National rule places transgender prisoners per gender identity; head of government committed to reviewing assignment; a 2022 study found officers generally attentive to trans-prisoner safety.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: Custody exposure is real but largely resident-sphere; a visitor facing arrest would encounter the identity-based placement rule and functioning courts.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: Two provinces enacted school-pronoun/healthcare rollbacks shielded by constitutional override clauses; these are resident/school-facing, not visitor facility rules. No visitor-facing facility exclusion documented.
federal_state_facilities.protection: Provincial human-rights codes cover gender identity and expression; one has published policy and case law giving a documented recourse route.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Override-clause statutes show some institutions working against trans interests, but no operative rule reaches a traveller's lodging, transport, or amenities.

care_services.exposure: Provincial health-statute rollbacks (one province, override-protected) signal possible friction; no documented denial of care to visitors.
care_services.protection: Gender identity/expression are protected grounds in the national human-rights act; 2016 reform removed the surgery requirement for document changes.
care_services.interaction: An emergency-care denial could be complained about under the national act or provincial code; enforcement record for visitors not documented.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: Hate crimes up six consecutive years (+169% since 2018); an advocacy group documents a rising organised anti-trans movement; two provinces rolled back school/health protections.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: Gender identity/expression are hate-motivation grounds in the criminal code (2017); 2024 hate-crime total rose only 1% and sexual-orientation incidents fell 26%.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: State framing is protective on paper; the growing movement raises the probability of street hostility the police then respond to under hate provisions.

minors_guardians.exposure: One province requires parental consent before a student under 16 may use a gender-related name/identity (override-clause law); affects enrolled students, not visiting minors.
minors_guardians.protection: Anti-bullying statutes covering LGBTQ students exist in nine listed jurisdictions; visiting families are outside school-enrolment rules.
minors_guardians.interaction: A travelling minor accompanying a trans parent faces no documented differential rule; resident school rules do not transfer to visitors.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: 2022 survey: 39% of 2SLGBTQI+ respondents reported identity-based violence in five years — 90% verbal, 17% physical; six-year hate-crime rise indicates elevated hostility, though the series lacks gender-identity disaggregation.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Hate-crime provisions cover gender identity; functional police/courts; 2024 sexual-orientation incidents fell 26%.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Social hostility is real but predominantly verbal; a traveller outed on the street can invoke hate-crime law in a rule-of-law state.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Two key 2024/2022 data pages were unretrievable; anti-trans hate-crime level unresolved; other provinces' document procedures unsourced — genuine unknowns, not exposures.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Documented functioning recourse: human-rights commission with published policy and case law; national act plus provincial codes; identity-based custody rule under litigation.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Remedies exist and operate; uncertainty concerns measurement and subnational variation, not the availability of redress.

anchor_checks.comparison: Far above: no Visitor Conduct Register, no entry bar, no state-engineered exclusion of trans visitors. The dossier documents the opposite — protected grounds, X markers, and a recourse commission. Exclusion/humiliation with no remedy is simply absent here.

Above: 0.55-B centres on discretionary border secondary screening and denied admission — the exact exposure this dossier's 'deliberately not counted' section says is undocumented. Residual similarity is bureaucratic inconsistency, but without documented screening friction the visitor's entry is materially cleaner.

Similar tier: both combine trained/protected frameworks with wide officer discretion and uneven practice. This dossier sits slightly higher on law (national hate-crime coverage, documented commission recourse) but lower on visitor-specific evidence (no border training or detention-appeal record), plus a rising hate-crime trend 0.75-C lacks.

Slightly below: 0.85-A documents prompt apologies, compensation and independent oversight functioning for a traveller. Here remedies are documented in the abstract but no incident-level proof of them operating for a trans visitor exists, while hate crime has risen six straight years and an organised anti-trans movement is growing.

parsed.synthesis: The operative regime for a traveller pairs strong, in-force legal protections (national human-rights act, criminal-code hate provisions, provincial codes with a documented commission route) with no documented visitor-facing restriction: no border screening, no facility exclusion, no criminalisation, identity-based custody placement. The deductions come from the social side — a six-year hate-crime rise, a 39% identity-based-violence prevalence figure dominated by verbal abuse, and a growing organised anti-trans movement — plus thin proof that remedies actually reach a short-stay visitor. Provincial override-clause rollbacks are resident/school-facing and do not transfer to the itinerary, but they mark a backsliding subnational edge. For an adult with a minor, school-consent laws apply only to enrolment; travelling families face no documented differential rule. Overall: reduced risk with a real, non-catastrophic hostility tail.
